The Bull Moose Party, officially the Progressive Party. Founded by former President Theodore Roosevelt in 1912 after his rupture with the Republican Party, it ran Roosevelt as its presidential candidate on a platform of social reform and progressive regulation of business.

Roosevelt formed the party after losing the Republican nomination to incumbent President Taft. This split the conservative Republican vote and guaranteed a Democratic victory. The party's symbol was the bull moose—Roosevelt famously claimed to be "as strong as a bull moose." The party attracted progressive reformers, many labor supporters, and women's suffrage advocates.

Roosevelt's 1912 campaign platform included workplace safety regulations, child labor restrictions, conservation initiatives, and antitrust enforcement. He received over 27 percent of the popular vote, the highest third-party showing until Ross Perot in 1992. Running on the slogan "A Chicken in Every Pot," the party promised expansive federal intervention in the economy to aid working people.

Though Roosevelt lost, the Progressive Party's split with the Republicans cemented a major realignment. Woodrow Wilson's Democratic victory ended a generation of Republican dominance since the Civil War. The party largely dissolved after 1912, though it ran a second time in 1916, again with Roosevelt, but won far fewer votes as Republicans reunified. The Bull Moose campaign stands as one of the strongest third-party showings in U.S. history and epitomized the reformist energy of the Progressive era.
